html:
Đại Việt, "Great Việt", was the name of the Vietnamese kingdoms that ruled from around present-day Hanoi from the 10th century until the early 19th. The chart's bar runs from independence in 939 to the French protectorate of 1884.

For about a thousand years, from the Han conquest of 111 BCE, northern Vietnam was a Chinese province. In 938 Ngô Quyền beat a Southern Han fleet at the Bạch Đằng River by planting iron-tipped stakes in the riverbed, and declared himself king in 939. The name Đại Cồ Việt was adopted in 968.

Its main dynasties:

  • Lý (1009 to 1225), which moved the capital to Thăng Long, now Hanoi, and founded the Temple of Literature.
  • Trần (1225 to 1400), which beat back three Mongol invasions sent by Kublai Khan.
  • Later Lê (from 1428), founded by Lê Lợi after he drove out the Ming, who had occupied the country from 1407.

Đại Việt modelled its state on China, with Confucian exams and Chinese characters, and paid tribute to Chinese emperors while calling its own ruler emperor at home. It also kept expanding south at the cost of Champa, the long "southward advance" that took Vietnamese settlers to the Mekong Delta by the 18th century.

From the 16th century rival lords split the country. The Tây Sơn brothers swept them away in the 1770s and 1780s, and Gia Long founded the Nguyễn dynasty in 1802 and in 1804 renamed the country Việt Nam. France took the south from 1859 and made the rest a protectorate in 1884, later part of French Indochina.
